title: Axiom-based specification (OBJ/CASL)
description: Algebraic specification defines data types by their operations and the equations between them — a stack is push/pop with pop(push(s,x)) = s, no implementation mentioned. Languages like OBJ and CASL let engineers write these axioms, and implementations are tested by checking they satisfy every equation.
method: Declare sorts and operations; write equations as axioms; test implementations by evaluating both sides of each axiom on random inputs.
usage: Specify the core data types algebraically; generate axiom tests automatically; run them against every implementation.

demo.code:
print('axiom: pop(push(s, x)) = s')
s = []
print('test: pop(push([], 1)) =', ([1].pop(), s)[1], '== [] -> HOLDS')

title: Initial algebra semantics
description: The initial-algebra approach says a specification denotes the 'most general' model satisfying its axioms — no junk (unreachable values), no confusion (distinct terms stay distinct unless axioms equate them). Testing against the initial model means checking the implementation adds nothing the spec didn't allow and identifies nothing the spec kept apart.
method: Construct the initial model (term algebra modulo axioms); test no-junk (every value reachable) and no-confusion (distinct normals stay distinct).
usage: Use initial semantics for data-type specs; test implementations for junk and confusion explicitly.

demo.code:
print('spec: stack with push/pop')
print('no-junk: every stack value = pushes from empty -> OK')
print('no-confusion: [1] != [2] (no axiom equates them) -> OK')

title: Narrowing-based test generation
description: Narrowing symbolically executes the spec's equations to generate test inputs that cover distinct behaviors — instead of random testing, it derives inputs guaranteed to exercise different rewrite paths. Fewer tests, better coverage, all derived from the algebra itself.
method: Apply narrowing to the spec rules; collect the generated substitutions as test inputs; run them against the implementation.
usage: Use narrowing-generated suites for the core algebra; supplement with random testing for robustness.

demo.code:
print('narrowing pop(push(s,x)): generates s=[], s=[a], s=[a,b]')
print('3 derived inputs cover all rewrite paths')

title: Algebraic property documentation
description: Axioms double as the best documentation: 'get(put(m,k,v),k) = v' tells a user exactly how a map behaves, precisely and completely. Specs written as equations are unambiguous, testable, and shorter than prose — documentation that can't lie because it's executed.
method: Document each operation by its equations with other operations; keep the axiom set minimal and complete; link axioms to their tests.
usage: Write axioms before prose; generate the docs' examples from the axiom tests.

demo.code:
print('map docs: get(put(m,k,v),k)=v; get(put(m,k,v),j)=get(m,j) for j≠k')
print('each equation links to its 200-case property test')

title: Modular specification composition
description: Big specs compose from small ones: a map spec imports a list spec, parameterized specs instantiate for element types. Compositional testing checks each module's axioms in isolation, then checks the composition — failures localize to one module instead of the whole edifice.
method: Write parameterized, importable spec modules; test each module's axioms; test composition points; reuse modules across projects.
usage: Modularize specs like code; test modules independently; version shared spec modules.

demo.code:
print('spec MAP imports LIST, parameter X')
print('test LIST axioms (300 cases) -> test MAP axioms (300) -> composition: OK')

title: Executable spec as oracle
description: When the algebra is executable (Maude, OBJ), the spec itself runs — and becomes the test oracle: feed the same inputs to spec and implementation, compare outputs. The spec is unambiguous, always current, and disagreements are either implementation bugs or spec bugs, both worth finding.
method: Execute the spec on test inputs; execute the implementation; compare; triage every disagreement.
usage: Keep the spec executable and fast enough for the test suite; triage disagreements promptly.

demo.code:
print('spec eval: top(push([1,2],3)) = 3')
print('impl eval: 3 -> AGREE (oracle confirms)')

title: Refinement checking (spec to code)
description: Refinement says the implementation may be more deterministic than the spec but must never do what the spec forbids. Refinement checking verifies this direction: every implementation behavior is a permitted spec behavior. It's the formal version of 'the code honors the contract'.
method: Formalize the spec's allowed behaviors; check implementation behaviors are a subset (via model checking or testing); report behaviors outside the spec.
usage: Write the spec loosely (allow implementation freedom), then check refinement strictly.

demo.code:
print('spec allows: {sorted, stable-sorted}')
print('impl always stable-sorts -> subset of allowed -> REFINEMENT HOLDS')

title: Behavioral equivalence testing
description: Two implementations can differ internally yet behave identically through their observable operations. Behavioral specs define equivalence via experiments (sequences of operations with observable results); testing checks that the implementation is behaviorally equivalent to the spec model on a generated experiment suite.
method: Define observable experiments; generate experiment sequences; compare spec model vs implementation outcomes; equivalence = identical observations.
usage: Generate experiments covering operation interactions; compare outcomes, never internal state.

demo.code:
print('experiments: push;push;pop;top on spec-model vs impl')
print('1000 generated experiments: all observations identical -> BEHAVIORALLY EQUIVALENT')
